Volume 06 · Chapter 04

Consumption, saving and investment

Undergraduate Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v06-c03

By the endDerive intertemporal decisions and connect household and firm behavior to aggregates.

Capability and prerequisites

After this chapter, you can derive a household's dated consumption plan, determine whether a credit limit binds, distinguish a revision in lifetime resources from a current receipt, and solve a firm's investment choice with depreciation and installation costs. You can then reconcile the choices with aggregate resource accounting without treating an accounting identity as a causal mechanism.

Read Innovation, human capital and institutions, using the accounts and capital timing in Chapter 1 and Chapter 2. We use constrained optimization, conditional probability and intertemporal price and income effects through consumer duality. All numerical cases below are synthetic. One period has a fixed length; returns, income flows and depreciation must refer to that same length.

1. Income arrives on dates; wealth buys a consumption path

A promised salary increase may affect spending before the first higher paycheck. A household unable to borrow may wait until the money arrives. Neither pattern follows from current income alone. Start with a model in which the timing is completely visible.

There are two dates, 0 and 1. All amounts are real units of one consumption good; its price is one at each date. Let a₀ be financial wealth already matured and available at date 0, y₀ and y₁ disposable nonasset income, and x₀ = a₀ + y₀ current resources. We take x₀ > 0 and y₁ ≥ 0. The household chooses current consumption c₀ and a financial position s purchased at date 0. Positive s is saving; negative s is borrowing. The certain gross real return is R = 1 + r > 0, identical for borrowing and lending. Thus R, rather than the net rate r, multiplies the principal.

Date 0: c₀ + s = x₀.
Date 1: c₁ + b = y₁ + Rs.
Credit rule: s ≥ −B, where B ≥ 0.
Terminal rule: b ≥ 0; no unpaid terminal debt.

Here s is the financial position carried forward. Allocating positive resources to that position is saving for the next date, but the position is not itself the household's saving flow when initial wealth is present. Under this dated allocation convention, y₀ − c₀ = s − a₀: a household can carry positive assets forward while running down its starting wealth. Accounting for interest income requires matching its earning date to the chosen income period.

The nonnegative terminal asset b has no utility and no subsequent use in this model. With strictly increasing utility of final consumption, any b > 0 can instead be consumed; hence b = 0 at an optimum. This is a consequence of the terminal objective and rule, not a universal assertion that people leave no wealth. A bequest motive, required bequest or another future period changes that step. Allowing unlimited unpaid terminal debt instead would let the household finance unbounded consumption without repayment.

Eliminate s and set b = 0:

c₀ + c₁/R = W, where W = x₀ + y₁/R,
and c₀ ≤ x₀ + B.

W is date-0 wealth, including the present value of future income. That future-income component is often called human wealth; it is not necessarily pledgeable collateral. The present-value equation alone forgets the credit rule, so satisfying it does not establish feasibility. The relative price of date-1 consumption is 1/R units of date-0 consumption. With a known inflation factor 1 + π and nominal gross return 1 + i, the matching real factor is R = (1 + i)/(1 + π); with uncertain inflation, that ratio is state dependent.

2. Euler conditions, inequalities and a global solution

Preferences are u(c₀) + βu(c₁), where β > 0 is the subjective weight on date 1, usually at most one. Initially assume u is twice differentiable on positive consumption with u′(c) > 0 and u″(c) < 0 throughout that domain. These conditions imply strict increase and strict concavity; the strict second-derivative condition is maintained explicitly. Define the utility from saving s by F(s) = u(x₀ − s) + βu(y₁ + Rs). Before differentiating, establish its domain:

s ≥ −B, s < x₀, and s > −y₁/R.
F′(s) = −u′(c₀) + βRu′(c₁).
F″(s) = u″(c₀) + βR²u″(c₁) < 0.

Our x₀ > 0, y₁ ≥ 0 and B ≥ 0 permit positive consumption at both dates: choose a sufficiently small positive s < x₀. A proposed borrowing limit may still be below the natural repayment boundary −y₁/R; that part of the nominal credit allowance is unusable with positive final consumption. If both income and initial resources were zero, positive consumption at both dates would be infeasible. Feasibility precedes an Euler equation.

At an interior optimum, increasing saving by a small amount sacrifices u′(c₀) utility per current unit and creates βRu′(c₁) discounted utility. Both directions of change are available, so

u′(c₀) = βRu′(c₁).

This is the Euler equation. It equalizes marginal utility costs and benefits across dates, not necessarily consumption levels. Strict concavity makes a feasible stationary point the unique global optimum. More generally, the tangent inequality gives F(s) − F(s*) ≤ F′(s*)(s − s*). At an interior root the right side is zero.

If the borrowing boundary s* = −B leaves both consumptions positive, only increases in s are feasible locally. Optimality instead requires F′(s*) ≤ 0. Introduce its nonnegative multiplier λ, measured in utility per extra unit of date-0 credit allowance:

u′(c₀) − βRu′(c₁) = λ ≥ 0,
s + B ≥ 0, and λ(s + B) = 0.

These are the relevant Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions. At the lower boundary, F′(s*) ≤ 0 and every feasible s − s* ≥ 0, so the same tangent inequality proves global optimality. A binding constraint may have λ = 0 exactly at the point where the unrestricted optimum touches it. A strict positive gap indicates a desire to borrow more. It is not evidence that the person miscalculated the interest rate.

Existence, zero consumption and a usable closed form

For u(c) = ln c, utility tends to minus infinity as either consumption approaches zero. On this bounded feasible interval a maximizing sequence therefore stays away from those excluded endpoints; continuity on the remaining closed interval gives attainment, and strict concavity gives uniqueness. Solving the interior Euler equation and budget yields

c₀ᵘ = W/(1 + β), c₁ᵘ = βRW/(1 + β),
sᵘ = (βx₀ − y₁/R)/(1 + β).
With the borrowing rule: s* = max{−B, sᵘ}, c₀* = x₀ − s*, c₁* = y₁ + Rs*.

The unrestricted log solution is strictly inside the two positivity boundaries; clipping it at −B cannot cross the upper boundary under our assumptions. For a utility function continuous at zero, the nonnegative-consumption feasible set is the closed interval [max{−B,−y₁/R}, x₀]. Continuity gives existence there, but a zero-consumption endpoint may win. Use the appropriate one-sided slope or compare endpoints. For linear u(c) = c, F has slope βR − 1: choose the upper endpoint if positive, the lower if negative, and every feasible point ties if it is zero. Strict concavity and log boundary behavior cannot be claimed for that case.

For power utility with marginal utility u′(c) = c−σ, σ > 0, an interior solution has c₁/c₀ = (βR)1/σ. Equal consumption follows when βR = 1. A larger R tilts the ratio toward later consumption, holding β and σ fixed; it need not increase the amount saved, because wealth and substitution effects also change the levels. The inspected MIT consumption notes develop the dated-budget and consumption-smoothing method; our explicit boundary proof and cases apply it to the stated feasible sets.

Worked example 1 — The present-value budget is not enough

A household has x₀ = 40, y₁ = 100, R = 5/4 and log utility with β = 1. Wealth is W = 40 + 100/(5/4) = 120. With sufficient credit, c₀ = 60, c₁ = 75 and s = −20. The two budgets read 60 − 20 = 40 and 75 = 100 − 25. Consumption grows because βR > 1.

Now permit borrowing of at most B = 8. The unrestricted plan fails that rule; the constrained choice is s = −8, c₀ = 48 and c₁ = 90. It still satisfies 48 + 90/(5/4) = 120. The multiplier is

λ = 1/48 − (5/4)/90 = 1/144 > 0.

Because F is strictly concave and F′(−8) = −1/144, any increase in saving lowers utility and further borrowing is infeasible. This certifies the global solution. A small extra unit of permitted borrowing raises c₀ by one and lowers c₁ by 5/4 while the limit remains binding. The multiplier is a marginal utility gain, not a dollar welfare measure.

With y₁ fixed, raising current resources x₀ by ε increases unrestricted current consumption by ε/2. Under the binding limit it increases c₀ by ε and leaves c₁ unchanged locally. Thus the marginal propensity to consume, the derivative of current consumption with respect to the specified resource change, depends on both the shock and the active constraint.

3. Permanent income and the life cycle

Extend the certain-income model to dates 0,…,T with a constant R. Let Aₜ be assets purchased at t, so c₀ + A₀ = a₀ + y₀ and cₜ + Aₜ = yₜ + RAₜ₋₁ for t ≥ 1. Set AT = 0 under the same no-bequest terminal rule. Multiplying each budget by R−t and summing cancels all intermediate asset positions:

Σₜ₌₀ᵀ cₜ/Rᵗ = a₀ + Σₜ₌₀ᵀ yₜ/Rᵗ = W₀.

With common strictly concave period utility, no binding interim credit constraints and βR = 1, adjacent Euler equations imply constant consumption. Its level is

c = W₀/HT, where HT = Σₜ₌₀ᵀ R−t.

HT is the price of one unit at every remaining date; c is the annuity value of total resources. This is a precise finite-horizon version of the permanent-income idea: planned consumption responds to sustainable resources, rather than mechanically equaling each paycheck. Life-cycle reasoning adds a changing remaining horizon and an income profile associated with schooling, work and retirement. Financial assets can bridge those dates. It does not predict that every household must borrow when young or dissave when old: credit, pensions, initial wealth, family needs, health, mortality and bequests can change the model.

A newly learned one-time increment Δ at date j raises W₀ by Δ/Rʲ and current consumption by Δ/(RʲHT). A newly learned increment Δ at every remaining date raises wealth by ΔHT and consumption by Δ. Here “permanent” means lasting across the stated remaining horizon. Both comparisons require that the news leaves interest rates, preferences, taxes, risk and all relevant constraints fixed. A payment already included in the plan is not new lifetime wealth when it arrives. Consumption may still follow its previously planned path; absence of new information does not require a flat path when βR differs from one.

Worked example 2 — Retirement, news and liquidity

At three dates a household with no initial wealth receives incomes (30,90,0). Let R = β = 1 and u = ln. With borrowing allowed, total resources 120 fund consumption (40,40,40). The asset sequence is A₀ = −10, A₁ = 40 and A₂ = 0: borrowing first, repaying and accumulating retirement assets next, then spending them.

If every Aₜ must be nonnegative, c₀ ≤ 30. At c₀ = 30, the remaining 90 is optimally divided into (45,45). The first-date saving derivative is −1/30 + 1/45 = −1/90 < 0, while the final two dates satisfy their Euler equality. Concavity of total utility on the linear feasible set certifies (30,45,45) globally; the assets are (0,45,0).

Return to unrestricted credit. A newly learned extra 12 at date 1 raises each planned consumption by 4, to 44. An extra 12 at all three dates raises each to 52. Under no borrowing, adding 12 only to date-1 income instead leaves current consumption 30 and raises the last two consumptions to 51. The future income is valuable in each case; access to it before receipt differs. These are conditional counterfactuals, not measured average responses.

4. Expectations and precautionary saving

Under uncertainty, an expectation is a probability-weighted average using the household's information at the decision date. In a finite-state two-period version, future nonasset income is Y₁ with stated probabilities, s is chosen before its realization, R is certain, and no insurance contract pays differently across states. Every state must leave positive consumption. Expected utility is

F(s) = u(x₀ − s) + β Σj pju(y1j + Rs),
with s ≥ −B, s < x₀ and s > −minj y1j/R.

There are finitely many states, all relevant probabilities are positive, and differentiating this finite sum gives the interior condition u′(c₀) = βR E₀[u′(Y₁ + Rs)]. At a binding borrowing boundary it becomes u′(c₀) ≥ βR E₀[u′(Y₁ + Rs)]. Strict concavity again supplies globality. Replacing the random income by its mean generally changes the answer, because the expectation applies to marginal utility.

Here is a sufficient precautionary-saving result with its scope exposed. Compare uncertain Y₁ with the certain income E₀Y₁, holding current resources, R, β, feasible constraints and insurance opportunities fixed. Suppose the certain-income optimum sᶜ is interior and leaves positive consumption in every risky state. If marginal utility u′ is strictly convex over those states, Jensen's inequality gives E₀[u′(Y₁ + Rsᶜ)] > u′(E₀Y₁ + Rsᶜ) for nondegenerate risk. The risky problem's F′ at sᶜ is therefore positive. Since that derivative decreases strictly in s, an attained interior risky optimum has sʳ > sᶜ: more saving and less current consumption.

For a three-times differentiable utility, u‴ > 0 is a sufficient local curvature condition for convex marginal utility; u″ < 0 alone is not. Binding constraints can prevent a strict response. General changes in variance that are not a mean-preserving spread, risky returns correlated with income, endogenous work, insurance and changes in credit are outside this comparison. Carroll and Kimball's inspected author manuscript discusses the marginal-value mechanism; we prove only the finite comparison just specified.

Worked example 3 — The same mean, a different saving decision

Let x₀ = 4, R = β = 1, u = ln and B = 1. If future income is certainly 4, the optimum is s = 0 and consumption is (4,4). Now future income is 2 or 6, each with probability 1/2. The feasible interval is −1 ≤ s < 4. At the certain-income solution, the risky derivative is −1/4 + (1/2)(1/2 + 1/6) = 1/12 > 0.

1/(4 − s) = 1/[2(2 + s)] + 1/[2(6 + s)]
⇒ 2s² + 8s − 4 = 0
⇒ s* = √6 − 2 ≈ 0.449490.

The other root is outside the domain. Current consumption is 6 − √6 ≈ 3.550510; final consumption is √6 or 4 + √6, each positive. The root lies above −1, so the credit constraint is slack. Strict concavity and the Euler equality certify the global choice. With log utility u‴(c) = 2/c³ > 0, the general precautionary argument applies. No simulation or large-sample approximation is needed.

Predictions and evidence. A rational-expectations restriction makes beliefs agree with the model's conditional distribution given available information; it does not give foresight of the realized state. A subjective-belief model instead specifies beliefs without that agreement. The saving calculation needs a distribution under either interpretation. Observed consumption alone does not identify that distribution, patience, risk aversion or access to credit. Even an observed Euler residual could reflect a binding constraint, measurement error, omitted needs or mistaken beliefs. A credible empirical design defines news and receipt dates, measures relevant resources and borrowing access, and uses a justified comparison or source of variation. It distinguishes a spending response from its proposed mechanism; see causal identification and behavioral evidence.

5. A firm buys capital before it produces

Households transfer purchasing power across dates; firms can also transform current goods into productive capital. We solve a finite project so that the last date has an explicit value rather than an unspecified continuation. Let K₀ be installed physical capital at date 0. It depreciates at fraction δ ∈ [0,1], and gross installation I at date 0 makes K₁ = (1 − δ)K₀ + I available for production at date 1. Investment is irreversible in this case: 0 ≤ I ≤ Ī, with a specified finite capacity Ī > 0. Existing capital cannot be sold at date 0.

At date 0 the firm pays p₀I for equipment and A(I) = φI²/2 for installation, with p₀ > 0 and φ ≥ 0. At date 1 it receives f(K₁), operating revenue net of all variable input costs; these costs must not be subtracted again. After that production, the capital has depreciated to (1 − δ)K₁ and is sold at the exogenous price p₁ ≥ 0. The firm can finance expenditure at the certain real gross rate R. No taxes, market-power effect on p₀ or p₁, financial rationing or risk premium is present.

V(I) = −p₀I − φI²/2 + [f((1 − δ)K₀ + I) + p₁(1 − δ)((1 − δ)K₀ + I)]/R.

All monetary amounts are in a common real purchasing-power unit, here real dollars. K and I are capital units; f is date-1 dollars, p is dollars per capital unit, and φ is date-0 dollars per squared capital unit. R is dimensionless. Current equipment and installation payments are not discounted; both future operating proceeds and sale proceeds are discounted once. The two appearances of depreciation refer to distinct intervals. New I is installed for date-1 production, then depreciates before its terminal sale. Different timing gives a different user cost.

For a differentiable concave f, V is concave; it is strictly concave if f is strictly concave or φ > 0. At an interior solution,

f′(K₁) + p₁(1 − δ) = R[p₀ + φI],
or f′(K₁) = UK + RφI,
where UK = Rp₀ − p₁(1 − δ).

UK is the date-1 user cost of one extra unit before installation costs: the financed purchase price minus its remaining resale value. When p₀ = p₁ = 1 it is r + δ, in date-1 goods per unit of capital. It is not always r + δ when equipment prices change. At I = 0 require V′(0) ≤ 0; at I = Ī require V′(Ī) ≥ 0. The tangent inequality proves globality in each case, including a nonzero slope at a constrained endpoint.

For f(K) = αK − γK²/2, with γ > 0 and this net-return function maintained over the feasible capital range, define k̄ = (1 − δ)K₀. Then

Iᵘ = [α − γk̄ + p₁(1 − δ) − Rp₀]/(γ + Rφ),
I* = min{Ī, max{0,Iᵘ}}.
V″ = −φ − γ/R < 0.

A negative unconstrained candidate calls for zero installation, not a negative value slipped past irreversibility. A binding spending limit would add a constraint such as p₀I + φI²/2 ≤ cash plus available credit, which can lower investment even with unchanged returns. If the firm is risk neutral and can discount all stated risky cash flows at this fixed R, replace future net proceeds by their expectations; with risk pricing or financing distress that replacement requires further theory. The inspected MIT investment notes supply the capital-timing, marginal-return and adjustment-cost method; our finite liquidation problem is derived here rather than attributed as their numerical example.

Worked example 4 — Install, retain or hit the limit

Take K₀ = 8, δ = 1/4, R = 5/4, p₀ = p₁ = 2, φ = 2/5, f(K) = 10K − K²/2 and Ī = 4. The inherited date-1 capital is k̄ = 6. Thus Iᵘ = [10 − 6 + 3/2 − 5/2]/[1 + 1/2] = 2, inside the bounds, and K₁ = 8. Marginal operating return is 2, user cost is 1 and RφI = 1, exactly reconciling the first-order condition.

At I = 2, equipment costs 4 and installation costs 4/5 now. Date-1 operating return is 48; terminal sale proceeds are 2(3/4)(8) = 12. Present value is −24/5 + 60/(5/4) = 216/5 = 43.2. At I = 0, operating return is 42 and sale proceeds 9, so V(0) = 204/5 = 40.8. These values include the inherited capital's proceeds; the value added by installation is 12/5.

V(I) − V(0) = (12/5)I − (3/5)I²
= 12/5 − (3/5)(I − 2)².

This identity independently proves the global maximum. If capacity is reduced to Ī = 1, install one unit: K₁ = 7, V = 213/5 and the increment is 9/5. The slope there is 6/5 > 0: the firm would expand if allowed. If φ were zero with the original capacity, the optimum would instead be I = 3. Convex installation costs reduce the chosen pace here; they are real costs, not a transfer to be added back to project value.

6. From individual choices to aggregate resources

Buying an existing share or bond exchanges a financial claim for money. By itself it installs no new machine and creates no new aggregate physical capital. A new security issue may finance subsequent production of capital, but issuing the claim and producing the equipment are different transactions. One household's loan is another entity's liability; both sides must be included when consolidating domestic financial positions. Asset revaluations also change wealth without being current saving.

For this paragraph, let C be private final consumption, G government consumption only, and Iaccounts all domestic gross investment, including government investment. This groups the same transactions differently from a table that includes government investment in G. In a closed economy, Y = C + Iaccounts + G then implies that gross national saving Y − C − G equals measured gross investment by accounting. This identity does not establish that an attempted increase in one household's saving produces an equal increase in output or machines. Prices, income, credit, other spending and investment plans must jointly satisfy market clearing. In an open economy, transactions with the rest of the world matter as well; later chapters add those accounts.

Keep the physical law Kₜ₊₁ = (1 − δ)Kₜ + Iphysical,t separate from valuation and classification. If an adjustment cost uses additional real resources, a one-good model's resource constraint must include them: Y = C + Iphysical + A(I) when all prices are one and government and trade are absent. If the accounting convention capitalizes those installation services, Iaccounts includes their value. Calling physical I alone national investment while silently discarding A(I) would break the ledger. Actual classification and measured capital stocks require the conventions in Chapter 1; our homogeneous-capital law is a stylized physical model.

Nor does adding identical-looking individual Euler equations automatically yield a representative household equation. Different income risk, marginal utilities, credit constraints and assets matter. Similarly, an investment–cash-flow correlation can arise from financing limits or because cash flow conveys information about future returns. Model equations organize these competing explanations; they do not identify one from correlation.

Exercises

  1. A credit limit and a growth condition. With log utility, β = 5/6, R = 6/5, x₀ = 30 and y₁ = 72, find the unrestricted consumption and saving plan. Impose B = 10, recalculate it and compute the borrowing multiplier. Show the dated and present-value budgets and give a global optimality argument. Does βR = 1 imply equal consumption under the limit?
  2. Boundary and terminal logic. Let u(c) = c on c ≥ 0, x₀ = 20, y₁ = 15, R = 11/10 and B = 5. Find all optimal saving choices for β = 1, β = 1/2 and β = 10/11. Explain why the log interior formula is inapplicable. In the original strictly increasing two-date model, explain how a required terminal bequest of 3 changes the lifetime budget, and why allowing unlimited unpaid terminal debt destroys the intended problem.
  3. Four-date life cycle and news. Take R = β = 1, log utility, zero initial wealth and incomes (18,66,48,0) at dates 0,1,2,3. Find consumption and all end-of-date assets with unrestricted credit and then with nonnegative assets at every date. For unrestricted credit, compute the consumption revision from newly learning before date 0 of an extra 12 only at date 1, or an extra 12 at every date. Under no borrowing, separately calculate the current-consumption response to an extra 12 at date 0 and to an extra 12 at date 1. Verify that the relevant limits remain binding or become slack.
  4. Risk aversion is not the whole precautionary argument. Let x₀ = 6, β = R = 1, B = 2 and future income be 3 or 9 with equal probabilities. With log utility, compare optimal saving against the certain-income-6 case; solve the quadratic and check feasibility. Repeat the comparison using u(c) = 20c − c²/2 on the feasible nonnegative consumption range. Explain the difference through marginal utility, and state why you cannot infer a strict response from concavity of u alone.
  5. A higher return with less saving. A household has x₀ = 60, y₁ = 0, β = 1 and u(c) = −1/c for c > 0. Borrowing is not needed. Derive its consumption and saving as functions of R > 0. Evaluate R = 1 and R = 4. Reconcile the change in the consumption ratio with the change in saving, and identify the error in “a higher return always raises saving.”
  6. Resale expectations and irreversibility. Use Worked example 4's original capacity Ī = 4 and all its parameters, but first raise the known date-1 resale price from 2 to 3. Find I, K₁ and the present-value gain over I = 0; then impose Ī = 2. In a separate case restore p₁ = 2 and replace operating return by f(K) = 6K − K²/2. Determine optimal installation and certify it globally. Explain why subtracting depreciation a second time from the already depreciated sale proceeds is wrong.
  7. Physical capital and the ledger. A synthetic closed economy has measured output 100, household consumption 90, no government or foreign transactions, equipment purchases worth 8 and installation services worth 2. All current prices equal one; the stated accounting convention capitalizes installation services. Physical capital starts at 50, depreciates at 10%, and increases through eight new equipment units; installation services do not add separate machine units. Residents also trade 30 of existing shares and make an internal loan of 6. Find measured gross investment, national saving and next physical capital. Reconcile the resource use, explain the role of the financial transactions, and assess the assertion “investment equals the increase in the physical stock.”
  8. What does one consumption observation identify? You observe x₀ = 40, c₀ = 48 and R = 5/4. Compare two log models with β = 1: A has certain future income 100 and borrowing limit B = 8; B has certain future income 70 and borrowing limit B = 30. Show that both predict the observation, identifying their planned final consumption and credit status. Does later realized income 100 necessarily reject model B if its date-0 belief was a forecast rather than literal certainty? Propose evidence that would help distinguish beliefs from credit constraints. Then give two explanations of a positive investment–cash-flow correlation and one design requirement for distinguishing them.
Complete solutions

  1. Wealth is 30 + 72/(6/5) = 90. Since 1 + β = 11/6, unrestricted c₀ = 540/11, c₁ = βRc₀ = 540/11, and s = −210/11. The dated budgets give c₀ + s = 30 and 72 + (6/5)(−210/11) = 540/11. The present value of consumption is (540/11)(1 + 5/6) = 90.

    The limit instead gives s = −10, c₀ = 40 and c₁ = 60. Now 40 − 10 = 30, 60 = 72 − 12, and 40 + 60/(6/5) = 90. The multiplier is 1/40 − (βR)/60 = 1/120 > 0. Strict concavity and F′(−10) = −1/120 prove global optimality on the feasible set. βR = 1 gives equal consumption only when the unconstrained Euler equality applies; the bound prevents the desired transfer to date 0.

  2. The nonnegative-consumption interval is [max{−5,−150/11},20] = [−5,20]. F(s) = 20 + 15β + (11β/10 − 1)s. At β = 1 its slope is 1/10, so uniquely s = 20, c₀ = 0 and c₁ = 37. At β = 1/2 the slope is −9/20, so uniquely s = −5, c₀ = 25 and c₁ = 19/2. At β = 10/11 the slope is zero: every s in [−5,20] is optimal. Linear utility has neither strict curvature nor a penalty tending to minus infinity at zero consumption; a log formula would solve a different objective.

    A required b ≥ 3 binds at b = 3 absent a bequest benefit, giving c₀ + c₁/R = x₀ + (y₁ − 3)/R along with all interim feasibility conditions. If b could be arbitrarily negative and repayment never occurs, fixing s while making b more negative raises c₁ without using genuine lifetime resources. For unbounded increasing utility such as log or this linear utility, the objective is unbounded. With bounded increasing utility one can instead lose attainment; neither case is the intended repayment problem.

  3. Lifetime resources are 132. Unrestricted consumption is 33 at every date, with assets (−15,18,33,0). Under no borrowing, current consumption cannot exceed 18. The remaining incomes total 114, permitting consumption 38 at each remaining date, with assets (0,28,38,0). The first intertemporal slope is −1/18 + 1/38 < 0 at the binding lower asset bound; later marginal utilities are equal. Strict concavity and these supporting inequalities establish globality.

    Unrestricted, extra income 12 once raises every consumption from 33 to 36. Extra 12 at each of four dates raises every consumption to 45. With no borrowing, an extra 12 only now changes incomes to (30,66,48,0): consume (30,38,38,38), assets (0,28,38,0). The all-date unrestricted level 36 would still exceed current resources 30, so the first constraint still binds; current consumption rises by 12. An extra 12 only at date 1 instead gives (18,78,48,0): consume (18,42,42,42), assets (0,36,42,0). The first constraint again binds and later ones are slack; current consumption does not rise. A once-only payment and a lasting stream are different wealth revisions.

  4. Certain future income 6 gives s = 0 and consumption (6,6). With risk, the log Euler equation is 1/(6 − s) = (1/2)/(3 + s) + (1/2)/(9 + s) = (6 + s)/[(3 + s)(9 + s)]. Hence 2s² + 12s − 9 = 0, with feasible root s = (3√6 − 6)/2 ≈ 0.674235. The other root is below −2. At the feasible root c₀ = 9 − 3√6/2, and final consumption is 3√6/2 or 6 + 3√6/2. The root is in (−2,6), leaves every consumption positive and satisfies a strictly concave objective's Euler equality.

    For quadratic utility, all feasible consumptions lie between 0 and 15, where u′ = 20 − c remains positive. The saving derivative is −[20 − (6 − s)] + E[20 − (Y₁ + s)] = −2s, exactly as in the certain-income case. The unique optimum is s = 0 in both. Risk subtracts Var(Y₁)/2 = 9/2 from expected future utility, independently of s. Utility is strictly concave but marginal utility is affine, so Jensen's marginal-utility inequality is equality. Strict risk aversion alone does not establish precautionary saving.

  5. Marginal utility is 1/c², giving c₁ = √R c₀. Since c₁ = Rs and c₀ + s = 60, s = 60/(1 + √R), c₀ = 60√R/(1 + √R), and c₁ = 60R/(1 + √R). All are positive for R > 0; the strictly concave objective tends to minus infinity at either zero-consumption endpoint, so the Euler solution is globally optimal.

    At R = 1, saving and both consumptions are 30. At R = 4, saving is 20, current consumption 40 and final consumption 80. The ratio rises from 1 to 2 even while saving falls by 10. The higher return buys more final consumption from fewer current units saved. The Euler tilt does not determine the total saving response without the resource equation and preferences.

  6. With resale price 3, k̄ = 6 and the installation numerator is 10 − 6 + 9/4 − 5/2 = 15/4. Its denominator remains 3/2, so I = 5/2 and K₁ = 17/2. The incremental present value is 3I − (3/5)I² = 15/4 − (3/5)(I − 5/2)². Thus the maximum gain is 15/4. With capacity 2, choose I = 2, K₁ = 8 and gain 18/5. The slope there is 3/5 > 0, certifying a binding upper limit.

    In the separate low-return case, with p₁ restored to 2, the numerator is 6 − 6 + 3/2 − 5/2 = −1. The formal candidate −2/3 violates irreversibility. The incremental objective is −(4/5)I − (3/5)I², strictly negative for every I > 0, so I = 0 uniquely maximizes value. Salvage already sells only (1 − δ)K₁; subtracting another δK₁ loss from those proceeds would double-count that same second-interval physical depreciation. The earlier depreciation from K₀ to k̄ is a different interval.

  7. Measured gross investment is 8 + 2 = 10 under the supplied capitalization convention. National saving is 100 − 90 = 10. Resources reconcile as 100 = 90 + 8 + 2. Physical next capital is (9/10)50 + 8 = 53, so the physical stock increases by 3. Gross equipment installation is 8, physical replacement is 5, and installation services are two additional current resource units that do not constitute separate machines.

    The existing-share trade changes ownership; the internal loan creates offsetting claims and liabilities. Neither adds another 30 or 6 to current aggregate investment. They can affect financing and distribution without being extra production. Investment is a flow; a net stock change subtracts depreciation and its valuation basis must match. The accounting investment value 10 cannot simply be inserted as ten new physical machines. No market-valued capital-stock change is supplied or inferable from the physical data alone.

  8. Model A's unrestricted saving is −20, so its borrowing bound forces s = −8, c₀ = 48 and planned c₁ = 90; its multiplier is 1/144. Model B has wealth 40 + 70/(5/4) = 96 and unrestricted c₀ = 48, s = −8, c₁ = 60. Since −8 > −30, its credit limit is slack and the Euler equation holds. Thus the same current observation is compatible with different expectations and constraints.

    If model B asserts literally certain income 70, a realization of 100 falsifies that certainty statement. If 70 was instead an expected value from a nondegenerate date-0 forecast, the realization alone does not refute the belief; the full distribution and its implications for expected marginal utility must then replace this certainty calculation. One may not silently retain the certainty formula for arbitrary risk. Useful evidence includes contemporaneous probability forecasts, announced versus received income, credit applications and limits, liquid assets, consumption measurement and an externally justified change in credit access or news. An experiment changing available credit can identify a response under its assignment and spillover assumptions; it does not by itself recover all preferences.

    A firm may invest more when cash flow relaxes a funding constraint, or because current cash flow forecasts more profitable demand. Distinguishing these requires variation that changes financing without independently changing investment returns, or a design measuring and credibly separating both channels. A simple cash-flow regression with an omitted return forecast cannot settle the mechanism. Grade this open portion for a specified contrast, observations, identifying assumption and concrete threat, rather than for choosing a particular research design.

Teach-back and delayed check

Teach-back: draw two dated household budgets and one dated firm cash-flow timeline. Derive the Euler equation using a feasible transfer, then show why the inequality changes at a borrowing limit. Explain why income arrival, income news, risk and an internal loan are four different objects. For the firm, explain why the terminal sale belongs in value and why an adjustment cost uses resources.

Teach-back checklist

A complete explanation shows c₀ + s = x₀ and c₁ = y₁ + Rs, names the terminal no-bequest assumption and checks positive consumption before moving resources. Saving one more unit costs u′(c₀) and benefits βRu′(c₁); equality needs both directions feasible, while a binding borrowing limit permits only more saving and therefore gives u′(c₀) ≥ βRu′(c₁). News revises a plan; receipt can implement old news or relax liquidity; risk specifies multiple possible outcomes; an internal loan transfers purchasing power and creates offsetting financial claims. The firm's current equipment/installation bill and next-date operating/sale proceeds belong on separate dates. Sale value is the explicitly available terminal payoff, and installation consumes additional resources rather than creating an offsetting financial claim.

Delayed check: after several days, solve the log household with β = R = 1, x₀ = 18, y₁ = 42 and B = 6. Give the unrestricted and constrained plans, the multiplier and a global certificate. For equipment with p₀ = p₁ = 1, R = 1.1 and δ = 0.2, state the date-1 user cost before adjustment costs. Explain why buying an existing bond does not itself increase the physical capital stock.

Delayed-check answer

Unrestricted wealth is 60, so c₀ = c₁ = 30 and s = −12. The credit bound instead gives s = −6, c₀ = 24 and c₁ = 36, preserving lifetime resources. The multiplier is 1/24 − 1/36 = 1/72; the strictly concave saving objective has negative derivative at the feasible lower boundary, proving global optimality. User cost is 1.1 − 0.8 = 0.3 date-1 goods per capital unit. An existing bond purchase transfers a claim; new production and installation must occur separately to add physical capital.

Reproduce and extend

The optional calculation lab supplies synthetic inputs, a standard-library Python program and a README. It solves the two-date log and finite quadratic investment cases, validates inputs and reports exact rational ledgers. Its assumptions are narrower than the entire chapter: it does not estimate beliefs or solve a general stochastic life-cycle model. The independent chapter checker additionally tests the risk example, boundary proofs, resource accounts and exercise arithmetic.

Carroll's inspected Fisher two-period notes provide another primary teaching route through the budget, Euler equation and income/substitution distinction. The source records identify the sections actually inspected; source inspection is separate from external validation of our original problems. Infinite-horizon transversality, precautionary wealth distributions, risk-adjusted capital pricing and structural estimation require further graduate study. The next planned chapter, Labor markets and unemployment, develops how employment and earnings are themselves determined; the y paths held fixed here will then become objects to explain.

Sources and further study

  • George-Marios Angeletos, MIT 14.05 — Consumption and Saving (Spring 2013) — Primary instructor method route for dated household budgets, terminal exhaustion without a bequest motive, intertemporal prices, the Euler condition, finite-horizon consumption smoothing and the limitation imposed by credit constraints. Original examples, boundary certificates and shock calculations are derived in the chapter.
  • Christopher D. Carroll — The Fisher Two-Period Optimal Consumption Problem (13 September 2023) — Primary author teaching route for the household's current resources, gross interest factor, terminal consumption, power-utility Euler solution and distinct substitution/wealth effects of an interest-rate change. The chapter's particular numbers and counterexample are original.
  • Christopher D. Carroll and Miles S. Kimball — Precautionary Saving and Precautionary Wealth (author manuscript) — Primary author method discussion of the saving flow versus accumulated precautionary wealth, dated cash-on-hand and expected marginal-value mechanism. The chapter independently proves a restricted two-date finite-risk comparison using convex marginal utility, rather than adopting an unconditional claim about every increase in risk.
  • Christian Wolf, MIT 14.05 — Lecture 18: Investment (Fall 2025) — Primary instructor method route for capital accumulation timing, marginal operating return and depreciation, convex investment adjustment costs and a financing constraint. The chapter derives its own finite project with dated equipment prices and terminal sale, including complete global boundary checks.
